PROPULSE BUSINESS

Precautions to reduce cracks in a new house

No practical building can be promised to remain completely crack-free. The goal is to reduce avoidable cracking through correct structural design, material control, workmanship, curing, movement detailing and timely inspection.

Construction precautions that can reduce the risk of cracks in a new house, including design, concrete quality, curing, joints, masonry, waterproofing and site supervision.

Start your requirement · Find professionals

Important

Wide, growing, diagonal or structural cracks should be assessed by a qualified structural professional. Cosmetic crack advice should not be used to diagnose structural safety.

01

Get the structure and foundation designed for the actual site

Soil conditions, spans, floor count, loads, openings and foundation behaviour affect cracking. Avoid copying reinforcement or footing details from another house.

02

Control concrete quality and water

Uncontrolled water addition, poor batching and weak compaction can increase shrinkage, segregation and defects. Use the specified concrete grade and approved mix/process.

  • Do not add water casually at site to improve workability
  • Compact concrete properly without over-vibration
  • Protect reinforcement cover and formwork dimensions
  • Plan pours so avoidable cold joints are reduced

03

Curing is a construction process, not a finishing step

Early moisture loss and hot-weather concreting can increase cracking risk. BIS lists IS 7861 (Part 1) for hot-weather concreting practice and IS 456 for reinforced concrete practice. Follow the project engineer’s curing method and duration.

04

Detail movement between different materials

Cracks often occur where RCC and masonry meet, around openings, long walls, chases and changes in geometry. Proper detailing, suitable mesh/reinforcement where specified, control joints where appropriate and sequencing can reduce recurring cracks.

05

Do not ignore masonry and plaster workmanship

Block/brick quality, mortar consistency, curing, chasing for services and plaster thickness can influence non-structural cracks. Coordinate electrical/plumbing chases before final plaster where possible.

06

Fix water ingress early

Leakage and repeated wetting can damage finishes and reveal or worsen defects. Roofs, toilets, balconies, external walls and plumbing penetrations need planned waterproofing and testing before finishes conceal them.
